subject: history_social
passage: From the fourteenth century onward, merchants of the Hanseatic League, an alliance of mainly German trading towns, dominated commerce in Bergen, Norway. Their chief export from the city was stockfish, cod caught off northern Norway and dried in the open air until it would keep for years. In return, the northern fishing communities, where cold, short summers made growing grain difficult, received grain shipped from Baltic ports. Historians usually explain the Hanseatic grip on Bergen by the merchants' control over the sale of stockfish to continental markets. Historian Solveig Hansen argues instead that their power rested mainly on grain: because the fishers depended on imported grain to survive, she contends, they had little choice but to sell their fish to the merchants who supplied it.
stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Hansen's argument?

choices.A: When English traders offered higher prices for stockfish but brought no grain, northern fishers still sold mostly to Hanseatic merchants.
choices.B: Hanseatic merchants in Bergen shipped more stockfish to German and Baltic ports than all other merchants there combined.
choices.C: Grain grew so poorly in northern Norway that few fishing families there could raise enough to last the winter.
choices.D: Northern fishers sold their stockfish to whichever merchants paid the most, whether or not those merchants supplied grain.

explanation.why: Hansen claims that the merchants' power came from supplying grain the fishers depended on, not from controlling stockfish sales. The best support would show fishers choosing the grain suppliers even when another buyer offered more for their fish. That behavior makes sense only if the need for grain, not price, bound the fishers to the Hanseatic merchants.
explanation.A: Correct. The fishers passed up better prices from traders who had no grain, which shows that dependence on grain tied them to the Hanseatic merchants.
explanation.B: Incorrect. This shows how large the merchants' stockfish trade was, which fits the usual explanation as well as Hansen's; it does not show that grain was the source of their power.
explanation.C: Incorrect. This explains why fishers needed imported grain, a point the text already makes, but it does not show that the need decided whom they sold to.
explanation.D: Incorrect. If fishers simply sold to the highest bidder regardless of grain, grain would not be the basis of the merchants' power; this weakens the argument.
